item.title: The Complexity of KKT Points of Quadratic Programs with Polynomially-Bounded Coefficients
item.description: arXiv:2611.03945v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Computing a Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) point of a quadratic polynomial over the unit hypercube is known to be $CLS$-complete, when the coefficients of the polynomial are encoded in binary. We prove that the problem remains $CLS$-complete even when the coefficients are encoded in unary. This is the first problem proven to remain $CLS$-hard when the input is given in unary.
item.dc:creator: Argyrios Deligkas, Michail Fasoulakis, Stavros D. Ioannidis

item.title: The Complexity of ReLU Network Synthesis from a Parameter Multiset
item.description: arXiv:2611.04074v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We ask how hard it is to build a neural network when its parameter values are given in advance. An instance supplies a multiset of rational numbers, a target behavior, and a bound on the number of neurons, output included. The question is whether one can choose the graph of a ReLU network within the bound, and place the numbers on its edges and biases so that it meets the target. This separates the numbers from the architecture; permutation training instead fixes the hidden units and only rearranges the output weights. Matching two labeled examples exactly is already $\mathsf{NP}$-complete; we ask what changes when the target must hold on every input or on average. Agreeing with a Boolean circuit on every Boolean input is $\Sigma_2^{\mathsf P}$-complete, already for four neurons. Agreeing with a given ReLU network on every real input lies in $\mathsf{DP}$ for every fixed neuron bound and is $\mathsf{DP}$-complete for three neurons. Approximating a ReLU network on the unit cube within absolute error one everywhere is $\Sigma_2^{\mathsf P}$-complete, even with no hidden neurons and all numbers equal and positive. Deciding whether some network has expected squared loss at most a threshold is $\mathsf{NP}^{\mathsf{PP}}$-complete for uniform Boolean inputs. For uniform inputs on the unit cube and for standard Gaussian inputs with a positive threshold, the same holds for two neurons when a positive risk gap, given in binary and possibly exponentially small, separates yes from no instances. Without a gap, the cube version is complete for guessing a polynomial-length string, then comparing a sum of exponentially many rationals with a threshold, all computable in polynomial time from the input and the guess. Since the graph is chosen too, the reductions must rule out every other network built from the same numbers.
item.dc:creator: Dimitrios Myrisiotis

item.title: On the Role of Geometry in Solving Variational Inequalities
item.description: arXiv:2611.04151v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The geometry of constraints in variational inequalities (VIs) plays a central role in applications ranging from resource allocation and equilibrium computation to constrained optimization. Yet, its effect on computational complexity has received surprisingly little attention beyond special cases. We examine this question when the constraint set is an $\ell_p$ ball. This family of problems encompasses two of the most extensively studied classes of problems in algorithmic game theory: symmetric bimatrix games for $p = 1$ and multi-player polymatrix games for $p = \infty$. Both of these problems are known to be PPAD-complete even for affine operators. We establish a comprehensive complexity landscape for VIs over $\ell_p$ balls across the full range $p\in[1,\infty]$. First, for any $p\neq 2$, we show that finding an inverse-polynomial approximate VI solution is PPAD-complete even for affine operators. In contrast, for $p=2$, we give a polynomial-time algorithm for affine VIs, extending a classic result of Ye (1992) beyond symmetric operators. On the other hand, once the operator becomes quadratic, we establish PPAD-completeness even at inverse polynomial precision. From a technical standpoint, we develop a new toolkit for exploiting the geometry of the constraint set and the structure of the operator to characterize the complexity of equilibrium and optimization problems, which is of independent interest.
item.dc:creator: Ioannis Anagnostides, Ioannis Panageas, Jingming Yan

item.title: Semidirect sums of tensors and the matrix multiplication exponent
item.description: arXiv:2611.04175v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This note is an exposition of the recent preprints from OpenAI that establish the bound $\omega \leq 9/4$ on the matrix multiplication exponent. We argue that the heart of these preprints is a new technique, which we formulate as the untwisting lemma for semidirect sums of tensors. This gives a generally applicable method for analyzing tensors. We also discuss further consequences of this method, as well as the relation between the OpenAI proof and previous work.
item.dc:creator: Baitian Li

item.title: Monodromy Computation Model
item.description: arXiv:2611.04377v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A closed path can return to its starting point while analytic continuation reaches another branch. We construct a finite computational calculus in which retained logarithmic branches supply memory, analytic observations select operations, and descent through a covering exposes deeper memory. Three branch coordinates suffice, and every finite observation uses the same cubic power covering. Each program defines a globally real analytic return map whose integer-lattice execution is realized by actual path lifting. Our first theorem simulates every finite-alphabet, finite-control Post--Turing machine, preserving complete configurations, halting, and divergence. Our second theorem identifies the partial numeric functions of the calculus, under fixed primitive-recursive input and output maps, with exactly the partial recursive functions. Deleting descent leaves a Forward language with a syntax-derived finite observation quotient and a primitive-recursive halting predicate. This yields a strict separation within the calculus and identifies access to deeper memory as its decisive additional operation. The constructions and semantic correspondences are formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib.
item.dc:creator: Xiaoyang Liu

item.title: Entropy-Weighted Soundness for Multi-Answer Birthday Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2611.04457v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The vertices of a Boolean birthday graph are partial assignments on $\ell$-subsets of $n$ variables. Although a satisfying assignment induces a $K$-clique for $K=\binom n\ell$, an arbitrary selection of $K$ vertices may repeat some views and omit others. This makes soundness substantially harder than under uniform view sampling. For bounded-occurrence, constant-gap Boolean ternary CSPs whose constraints each involve three distinct variables (allowing arbitrary Boolean predicates), we prove that the graph's maximum induced $K$-vertex density satisfies \[ \rho^*(K)\le 2\exp\!\left(-c\, \frac{\ell^3}{n^2\log(en/\ell)}\right) \] for $2\le\ell\le x_0n$ and $\ell\log(en/\ell)\ge C_0\log(n+1)$, with positive constants depending only on the source parameters. The argument refines the biclique counting method by charging the entropy of an adversarially chosen flattening to mutual information and a combinatorial obstruction energy. In the overlapping parameter range it strengthens the explicit soundness exponent previously established for this graph. We also establish an unconditional stability theorem for arbitrary sets $H$ of exactly $K$ distinct local assignments, with missing views and multiple answers: $f_*(H)\le34(n/\ell)q_{\mathrm{con}}(H)$ for every $1\le\ell\le n$. It gives a complementary additive near-clique soundness bound. We do not derive a new fine-grained hardness theorem.
item.dc:creator: Alexandru Popa

item.title: Abelian embeddings make useful promises: approximation of detrivialised equations
item.description: arXiv:2611.04569v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the following family of search problems: given a system of equations $x+y+z\equiv 0\pmod p$ promised to admit a solution that is nonconstant on every equation, find a $c$-colouring of the variables that makes no equation monochromatic. For $p\in\{2,3\}$, the problem recovers known tractable Promise Constraint Satisfaction Problems (PCSPs). For $p > 3$, we obtain a complete complexity classification: the problem is polynomial-time solvable for $c \geq 4$, yet even its decision version is NP-hard for $c = 3$, and it is not well-defined for $c = 2$. Our main conceptual contribution is a general tractability framework for PCSPs based on Abelian embeddings, a notion introduced by Bhangale, Khot, and Minzer [STOC 2022] in the study of quantitative approximation of satisfiable CSPs. We show that suitable Abelian embeddings yield polynomial-time PCSP reductions realised by singleton algorithms in the sense of Zhuk [FOCS 2026]. On the hardness side, the promise relation is far removed from the reconfigurable regime covered by the conditional hardness framework of Banakh, Barsukov, and Nakajima [LICS 2026]; our proof instead relies on a new additive-combinatorial rigidity theorem classifying special $3$-colourings of $\mathbb{Z}_p$.
item.dc:creator: Tamio-Vesa Nakajima, Zephyr Verwimp, Stanislav \v{Z}ivn\'{y}

item.title: Lower Bounds for Adaptive Relaxed Locally Decodable Codes via the Capped Horvitz--Thompson Estimator
item.description: arXiv:2611.04678v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove a nearly optimal lower bound on the blocklength of general relaxed locally decodable codes (RLDCs), extending the result of [GGS26] to nonlinear encodings and adaptive decoders with two-sided error. Namely, we show that any $q$-query RLDC $C\colon \{0,1\}^k \to \{0,1\}^n$ must satisfy $n = k^{1+\Omega(1/q)}$, closely matching the upper bound of $n = k^{1+O(1/q)}$ by Ben-Sasson, Goldreich, Harsha, Sudan, and Vadhan (STOC 2004). Our proof reduces showing RLDC lower bounds to estimating the output distribution of adaptive decoders. To this end, we introduce a capped Horvitz--Thompson estimator with uniformly bounded discrete derivatives on the $p$-biased cube. We establish its concentration of measure via self-bounding inequalities and control the downward bias induced by capping through a spreadness argument.
item.dc:creator: Guy Goldberg, Tom Gur, Sidhant Saraogi

item.title: Hardness Self-Amplification in Linear Algebra and Fine-Grained Cryptography
item.description: arXiv:2611.04680v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the possibility of basing fine-grained cryptography on the hardness of fundamental problems in linear algebra. Our main technical contribution is a hardness self-amplification method based on random low-rank updates: we show how to turn an algorithm that solves an inverse-polynomial fraction of random linear systems into a solver which succeeds for every right-hand side of almost every matrix. Our reduction increases the runtime only linearly in the inverse of the original success probability. In particular, this yields fine-grained one-way functions from the almost worst-case hardness of linear systems over large enough fields. Using the same approach, we also obtain tighter worst-case to average-case reductions for matrix multiplication and online matrix-vector multiplication, as well as variants of our reductions that recover exact solutions from approximate algorithms, whose expected coordinate agreement is only $1/q+\varepsilon$, with inverse-quadratic dependence on $\varepsilon$ up to logarithmic factors, over every finite field. Finally, we also use it to connect the existence of fine-grained key agreement to the problem of computing the rank of a matrix: over a suitable sequence of growing characteristic-two fields, the almost-everywhere average-case hardness of rank computation (for any of a large class of distributions) implies infinitely-often fine-grained key agreement.
item.dc:creator: Geoffroy Couteau, Nikolas Melissaris, Thejas Radhika Sajith

item.title: Information Loss Is All You Need: $TC^0$ Pseudorandomness from Worst-Case Lattices
item.description: arXiv:2611.05136v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Can deterministic information loss yield post-quantum pseudorandomness with $TC^0$ evaluation? We show that deterministic rounding achieves this under quantum worst-case lattice hardness, with fixed polynomial parameters and no predetermined sample bound. We introduce learning with algebraic rounding (LAR), which applies an explicit integer rounding map to blocks of secret-dependent linear measurements and encodes the result in a lattice quotient. For one fixed family with polynomially bounded modulus and dimensions, deterministic labels on exactly uniform, secret-independent public matrices are computationally indistinguishable from independent uniform labels for every polynomial number of classical random examples. Our classical reduction from Gaussian LWE, combined with the quantum worst-case reduction to LWE, bases LAR on GapSVP and SIVP over general lattices at approximation factor $\widetilde{O}(q)$, where $q$ is the modulus. The proof uses source-independent affine transport: public affine maps sampled independently of the hidden errors transport the Gaussian error law close to uniform on the rounding map's zero-label fiber while preserving exactly uniform public matrices. For every fixed inverse-polynomial accuracy, we give a polynomial-time sampler for the same public parameter family. This yields the first post-quantum weak pseudorandom function with joint key-and-input evaluation in $TC^0$, secure against uniform quantum polynomial-time distinguishers given any polynomial number of classical uniform random examples. We also prove hardness of learning polynomial-size two-hidden-layer ReLU networks from noiseless uniform random examples, even for quantum polynomial-time improper learners.
item.dc:creator: Chen Qian

item.title: The sum-of-squares complexity of linear-algebraic principles
item.description: arXiv:2611.05250v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the degree needed for sum-of-squares (SoS) proofs of several basic principles of real linear algebra. For any $n\times n$ matrix $A$ of rank greater than $r$, the Weak Rank Principle states that the equations $XY^\top=A$ with $n\times r$ matrix variables $X, Y$ have no solution. We show that this principle requires degree exactly $2r+2$ to prove. On the other hand, for $A=I_n$, setting $X = Y$ gives the Tight Frame Principle, which has a degree-$4$ proof. For $n\times n$ matrices, proving that a right inverse is also a left inverse requires degree exactly $2n+2$, while proving that orthonormal rows imply orthonormal columns again has a degree-4 proof. Using our lower bounds, we also derive related SoS degree lower bounds for polynomial systems encoding sign rank, matrix rigidity, small-width homogeneous non-commutative algebraic branching programs, and tensor CP rank. Lastly, we show that quantitative bounds on the Frobenius norms of the factors in the Weak Rank Principle can lower the degree required to refute $XY^\top=I_n$, but sufficiently large bounds still preserve the exact degree $2r+2$ from the unbounded case, giving a quantitative version of the Archimedean property arising in classical results on SoS proofs.
item.dc:creator: Dmitriy Kunisky, Xifan Yu

item.title: Some algebraic and geometric computations in CH via Chow forms
item.description: arXiv:2611.05289v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The problem of decomposing an algebraic variety into more structured components (such as equidimensional, irreducible, or connected components) is a fundamental problem in computer algebra and algebraic geometry. In this work, we study the computational complexity of computing equidimensional components of algebraic varieties, represented via Chow forms. We improve the state-of-the-art complexity bounds from PSPACE to CH, the counting hierarchy, for a number of problems related to equidimensional decomposition, including deciding (1) whether the Chow form of the $k^{\text{th}}$ equidimensional component of a given projective variety vanishes at a given point, (2) whether a given monomial is in the support of the Chow form of the $k^{\text{th}}$ equidimensional component of a given projective variety, (3) membership in a given equidimensional component of a given algebraic variety, and (4) membership in the closure of the image of an irreducible variety under a polynomial map. As an application of our algorithm to decide membership in the closure of the image of a variety under a polynomial map, we show that the approximate polynomial satisfiability problem can be decided in CH. We also show that the degree of the $k^{\text{th}}$ equidimensional component of a given projective variety can be computed in $\text{FP}^{\text{CH}}$. Our main technical result is the construction of a polylogtime-uniform family of constant-depth, exponential-size threshold circuits that compute the Chow forms of the equidimensional components of a given projective variety. We construct these circuits by combining the machinery of geometric resolutions together with the uniform constant-depth, exponential-size threshold circuits of Andrews, Garg, and Schost (FOCS 2026) for the multivariate resultant.
item.dc:creator: Robert Andrews, Abhibhav Garg, Rafael Oliveira, \'Eric Schost

item.title: TFNP in the Random Oracle Model
item.description: arXiv:2611.05308v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We determine which major $\TFNP$ classes are hard in the random oracle model (ROM). Prior work establishes average-case hardness of highly structured subclasses of $\TFNP$ from strong cryptographic assumptions such as LWE and indistinguishability obfuscation. It is not known whether weaker assumptions such as one-way functions imply hardness of any of the standard $\TFNP$ subclasses, even in the worst case. The ROM, where all parties have query access to a random function, lies, morally, between these two regimes: a random function is one-way, but public-key cryptography cannot be built from it in a black-box way. We refer to this setting as \emph{Romantica}. Our first result settles a long-standing open problem: $\PPAD$, the class of total search problems reducible to finding a Nash equilibrium, is hard on average in Romantica. Combined with the known hardness of PLS (local search), this gives average-case hardness of $\EoPL = \PPAD \cap \PLS$. In contrast, we show that $\UEoPL$ can be solved in Romantica with polynomially many oracle queries by a computationally unbounded solver, a sharp distinction between $\EoPL$ and $\UEoPL$. This resolves the black-box hardness landscape of all major $\TFNP$ classes in Romantica. Finally, we initiate the study of separations between $\TFNP$ subclasses in Romantica: $\PWPP$ and $\PPA$ do not reduce to $\PLS$ under \emph{public-coin} reductions.
item.dc:creator: Noah Fleming, Mika G\"o\"os, Ziyi Guan, Oliver Korten, Daniel Mitropolsky, Toniann Pitassi, Artur Riazanov, Dmitry Sokolov, Tianqi Yang, Weiqiang Yuan

item.title: A King for Almost Everyone
item.description: arXiv:2611.03838v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A tournament is an orientation of a complete graph. A vertex $v$ controls a vertex $u\neq v$ if there is a directed path of length at most two from $v$ to $u$, and a $\delta$-king is one that controls at least $\delta(n-1)$ vertices. In the query complexity model, each query reveals the orientation of an edge. Shen, Sheng and Wu [SICOMP'03] established an $\Omega(n^{4/3})$ lower bound on the deterministic query complexity of finding a $1$-king, and a non-matching upper bound of $O(n^{3/2})$. Neither bound has been improved in over two decades, despite substantial progress on variants of the problem. For $\delta$-kings with $\delta < 1$, Biswas, Jayapaul, Raman and Satti [Discrete Applied Mathematics'22] showed that $O(n^{4/3})$ queries suffice to find a $\frac12$-king. Lachish, Reidl and Trehan [FSTTCS'22] improved this guarantee to $\frac12+\frac{2}{17}$ using $\widetilde{O}(n^{4/3})$ queries, and asked whether a larger fraction could be achieved within the same query bound. We answer this question affirmatively for every fixed fraction below one: for every fixed $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, we give a deterministic algorithm that finds a $(1-\varepsilon)$-king using $O(n^{4/3})$ queries. The design of our algorithm is informed by a structural analysis combining a sparse regularity lemma due to Allen, Kohayakawa, Mota and Parente [Electronic Journal of Combinatorics'14] with a new sampling argument based on a reachability theorem of Afek, Gafni and Linial [arXiv'19].
item.dc:creator: Ziad Ismaili Alaoui, Oded Lachish, Nikhil S. Mande

item.title: On the optimality of truncation among binary linear sketches
item.description: arXiv:2611.03979v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study statistical inference and function evaluation problems in which the input binary vector is available only through a binary linear sketch, i.e., a fixed number of parity measurements. We show that under a certain monotonicity condition, simply truncating the input by retaining a subset of its coordinates is optimal among all linear sketches of the same size. In particular, this applies to distributed testing of correlations of binary vectors when they are of opposite signs and evaluating unate Boolean functions on uniformly random inputs. Additionally, given that truncation is optimal, we immediately have lower bounds for arbitrary binary linear sketches. To illustrate this application, we consider the one-way communication complexity of a distributional graph connectivity problem on $n$ vertices and show that truncation, and hence all binary linear sketches, requires $\Theta(n \log n)$ bits to achieve constant error, while a nonlinear protocol only requires $O(\log n)$ bits.
item.dc:creator: Robinson D. H. Cung, Adway Girish, Emre Telatar

item.title: On the (Quantum) Communication Complexity of Secure MPC from a Random Oracle
item.description: arXiv:2611.04052v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Information-theoretic MPC among $n$ parties with $t$ corruptions can securely evaluate a circuit $C$ with $O(|C| \cdot t/(n-t))$ online communication in the preprocessing model and $O(|C| \cdot t/(n-2t))$ communication in the honest majority setting. Damg{\aa}rd, Larsen and Nielsen (CRYPTO 2019) showed that both communication bounds are tight for inner products. Fully homomorphic encryption and other assumptions known to imply public-key cryptography beat both communication bounds, but the communication complexity with symmetric-key cryptography alone is less understood. For MPC with preprocessing, we prove that the same $\Omega(|C| \cdot t/(n-t))$ lower bound holds in the random oracle model, so a random oracle cannot reduce the online communication. For honest majority MPC relative to a random oracle, we present an $\Omega(|C|)$ communication lower bound that is matched by a new construction for degree-2 polynomials (including inner products) when $n = O(\log \lambda)$, beating the information-theoretic bound. We also study quantum MPC. First, we prove that information-theoretic protocols with quantum communication (and preprocessing) cannot reduce communication compared to their classical counterparts. Furthermore, we extend our lower bound for MPC with preprocessing to protocols with a quantum-accessible random oracle, but use only classical communication. In contrast, with both quantum communication and a post-quantum one-way function, we present a simple two-party protocol that evaluates the two-party instance of these circuits with $\mathrm{poly}(\lambda, \log |C|)$ communication, beating these lower bounds. Finally, such communication savings do not come for free. We prove that there exist circuits $C$ such that every blackbox protocol with $o(|C|)$ quantum communication must perform $\Omega(|C|)$ cryptographic operations.
item.dc:creator: Alexander Hoover, Giuseppe Persiano, Kevin Yeo

item.title: State Evolution and Universality of Iterated Linear Programs for the Binary Perceptron
item.description: arXiv:2611.04294v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The binary perceptron is a random constraint satisfaction problem that asks for a sign vector satisfying a system of random linear inequalities. Its solution space has a strikingly extreme geometry: at every positive constraint density, all but a vanishing fraction of the solutions are isolated. Yet polynomial-time algorithms find solutions at small enough constraint density, which raises the question of how efficient algorithms navigate such a landscape. Linear programming is a natural algorithm to study here, but its analysis has so far been limited to a single round. Li, Schramm, and Zhou (STOC 2025) analyzed one linear program followed by iterative rounding. In this work, we overcome this limitation and give a precise analysis of iterated linear programming for the binary perceptron. (1) For Gaussian matrices and any fixed number of rounds, we characterize the iterated linear programs exactly through a deterministic state-evolution recursion. (2) Adding a final rounding step, we obtain a randomized polynomial-time algorithm for the binary perceptron. Numerical evaluations of the recursion provide evidence that it succeeds at constraint density $\alpha=0.60$ with zero margin, well beyond the range $\alpha\le0.1$ guaranteed by the single-LP analysis and $\alpha\approx0.327$ (Jo and Lee, 2026), the best guarantee so far. (3) We establish universality, showing that the same characterization holds for matrices with i.i.d. entries drawn from any centered, unit-variance subgaussian law. The key idea of our proof is that, although conditioning on earlier rounds makes the matrix non-Gaussian, its conditional law can be computed explicitly and remains close to a Gaussian law, so the convex Gaussian min-max theorem applies in every round. For universality, we compare Gaussian and subgaussian matrices through the Lindeberg principle, using a regularized version of each linear program.
item.dc:creator: Jianan Zhang, Shuangping Li

item.title: Space-Optimal Algorithms for Spanning Forests in Dynamic Streams at Every Confidence Level: With and Without Deletion Constraints
item.description: arXiv:2611.04365v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We characterize the optimal space for one-pass spanning-forest computation in dynamic streams of $v$-vertex simple graphs with failure probability at most $\delta$. Nelson and Yu proved an $\Omega(v\log^2v\log(v/\delta))$-bit lower bound, establishing the AGM algorithm's optimality for each fixed $0<\epsilon<1$ and $2^{-v^{1-\epsilon}}<\delta\le1/4$. We resolve the remaining high-confidence regime: for every $0<\delta\le1/4$, matching lower bounds and an algorithm give \[ \Theta\!\left(\min\left\{v^2,\;v\log(v/\delta)\log^2\!\left(2+\frac{v}{\log(v/\delta)}\right)\right\}\right) \] bits, improving space by up to a factor of $\Theta((\log v/\log\log v)^2)$ in this regime. We also study streams with at most $Z$ previously inserted edges deleted and not yet reinserted at report time, where the integer $Z\ge0$ is given in advance. Total deletions, restorations, and intermediate absence counts are unrestricted. For a single report and every $0<\delta\le1/4$, matching lower bounds and a one-pass randomized algorithm yield optimal space $\Theta(\mathcal L(v,Z,\log(1/\delta)))$ bits, where $x_Z(t)=\min\{Z+1,v,\sqrt{vt}\}$ and \[ \mathcal L(v,Z,t)=v\log v\min\{\log^2v,\log^2(Z+2)\} +vt\log\!\left(1+\frac{x_Z(t)}t\right)\log\!\left(1+\frac v{x_Z(t)}\right). \] At zero error, a lower bound for all zero-error algorithms and a matching deterministic algorithm give optimal space \[ \Theta\!\left(\min\{v^2,v(Z+1)\log(1+v/(Z+1))\}\right) \] bits. Together, these results characterize the memory required across all confidence levels and report-time edge-loss bounds.
item.dc:creator: Zemin Chao, Jianhe Cen, Hengzhao Ma, Hongzhi Wang

item.title: On the Hardness of Approximate Quantum Circuit Membership and Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2611.04381v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Quantum circuit optimization is an indispensable component of the quantum software stack, used to reduce noise, maximize performance, alleviate costs of quantum error correction, or target specific hardware. A related problem is approximate membership: for a fixed set of unitaries $S$, decide whether a given circuit $C$ is within distance $\varepsilon$ of a unitary in $S$ under some metric $m$. Membership is a special case of optimization, where $S$ is a set of unitaries implementable at no cost (e.g., with noise-minimal circuits, or without magic states). Janzing, Wocjan, and Beth (Int. J. Quantum Inf., 2005) showed that, for the operator metric, the case $S=\{I\}$ (approximate identity) is QMA-complete when $C$ is promised to be either close to the identity or far from it. We generalize this setting in three directions: (i) promise-free inputs, (ii) besides $S=\{I\}$, sets $S$ containing only Clifford unitaries, or only generalized permutation matrices (i.e., no superposition), and (iii) the trace-based, spectral, and operator metrics. We show that, in all cases, approximate membership is PP-hard for wide ranges of $\varepsilon$, provided $C$'s gate-set can implement Clifford+T, as the gate-sets of standard hardware do. If $S=\{I\}$, or if $S$ contains only generalized permutation matrices, $I\in S$, and $m$ is a trace-based distance, PP-hardness holds for all non-trivial $\varepsilon$. If $S=\{I\}$ and $m$ is a trace-based distance, PP-hardness holds even for circuits over classical-reversible gate-sets. Our results indicate that approximate membership is harder over promise-free inputs than the QMA-complete promise version, and that this hardness persists across quantum resources (any gates, non-Clifford, superposition) and distance metrics. They directly imply PP-hardness of circuit optimization when minimizing total, non-Clifford, or superposition gate depth or count.
item.dc:creator: Adam Husted Kjelstr{\o}m, Jaco van de Pol, Andreas Pavlogiannis

item.title: Binary Huffman Coding with Unequal Letter Costs Is NP-Complete
item.description: arXiv:2611.04444v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Binary prefix coding assigns prefix-free binary words to symbols to minimize their frequency-weighted cost. Huffman solved the equal-letter-cost case in polynomial time in 1952 [Proc. IRE'52]. For unequal letter costs, Karp gave an integer-programming formulation in 1961 [IRE Trans. Inf. Theory'61]. Exact polynomial-time algorithms for fixed integer costs were given by Golin and Rote [IEEE Trans. Inf. Theory'98] and Bradford, Golin, Larmore, and Rytter [J. Algorithms'02]. For input-dependent costs, Golin, Mathieu, and Young gave a polynomial-time approximation scheme [SICOMP'12]. The exact complexity when letter costs are part of the input had remained unresolved. We resolve this $65$-year-old problem by proving that deciding whether there exists a binary prefix-free code of frequency-weighted cost at most a given threshold is NP-complete, even when the letter costs are consecutive positive integers $(M,M+1)$ supplied as part of the input. All frequencies, letter costs, and thresholds are encoded in binary. Consequently, finding an optimal code is NP-hard. Our proof uses two polynomial-time reductions, starting from Planar Independent Set. The intermediate problem prescribes the number of leaves at each depth of a full ordered binary tree and minimizes a signed linear score on their sorted right-edge counts. The first reduction represents an independent-set verification program by a tree growing level by level. A fixed-profile identity converts narrow coordinate restrictions into linear penalties that enforce the computation. The second reduction adds large dyadic terms to the symbol frequencies to force prescribed depths. These terms contribute a constant to the weighted number of ones, leaving smaller signed perturbations to reproduce the tree score.
item.dc:creator: L. Sunil Chandran, Rishikesh Gajjala

item.title: On the Complexity of Exact Autobidding Equilibria
item.description: arXiv:2611.04475v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Autobidding equilibria link advertisers' value multipliers or participation probabilities through aggregate budget and return-on-investment (ROI) constraints. We establish the exact computational complexity of finding these equilibria across several canonical settings: exact equilibrium computation is $\mathsf{FIXP}$-complete for second-price ROI pacing, budget- or ROI-constrained generalized second-price (GSP) sponsored shopping, and second-price throttling. Furthermore, approximating the equilibrium control vector in distance to a true equilibrium is $\mathsf{FIXP}_{a}$-complete when the target accuracy is provided as input.
item.dc:creator: Yiyang Huang, Zhengyang Liu, Yonglei Yan

item.title: Differentially Oblivious Priority Queues with Sublogarithmic Cost
item.description: arXiv:2611.04776v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In this paper, we study exact online integer priority queues under differential obliviousness in the balls-and-bins model. Given a public upper bound $T$ on the number of operations and assuming that the priorities are bounded by a polynomial in $T$, we construct an $(\eps,\delta)$-differentially oblivious priority queue supporting insertion and minimum extraction, which requires $\polylog(T)$ private memory. For constant $\varepsilon>0$ and $\delta=\exp(-\Theta(\log^2 T))$, our construction incurs $O(\log T/\log\log T)$ expected amortized total work per operation, which breaks the $\Omega(\log T)$ barrier for fully oblivious priority queues~[Jacob et al., SODA'2019]. Further, we prove a matching lower bound for $(\eps,\delta)$-differentially oblivious priority queues with $\varepsilon=O(1)$ and $\delta=o(1)$, which indicates that our construction is asymptotically optimal in terms of total work.
item.dc:creator: Zimai Guo, Cheng Hong, Zhechen Li

item.title: A Short Proof and Generalization of the Rainbow Cycle Theorem and Improved Bounds for Binary Even-Query LCCs
item.description: arXiv:2611.05034v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A \emph{rainbow cycle} in a list-edge-colored graph is a cycle where no color appears more than once. We give a short and simple proof of a result of [ABSZZ] showing that a properly edge-colored $n$-vertex graph with average degree $\Omega(\log n\log\log n)$ always contains a rainbow cycle, and generalize it to weighted graphs with edges list colored with list size at most $\ell$ and where the total weight of all edges containing a given color $i$ incident to a vertex is at most $\Delta$, showing that $\Omega_\ell(\Delta\log n\log\log n)$ average degree guarantees a rainbow cycle. Using the reduction of [AG26] and the new generalized rainbow cycle theorem, we prove that for $r\geq 3$, every binary linear $r$-query locally correctable code $E:\mathbb{F}_2^k\rightarrow \mathbb{F}_2^n$ satisfies $k\leq \tilde{O}(n^{1-2/(r-1)})$ by showing a rainbow analogue of the odd $r$-LDC lower bounds of [BHKL25,JM25], closing the gap between the best known lower bounds for odd- and even-query binary linear $r$-LCCs.
item.dc:creator: Andrew D. Lin

item.title: Finding Hypercliques Faster Than Brute Force
item.description: arXiv:2611.05082v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We show that for any fixed $k$, there exists $\varepsilon_k > 0$ such that, given a $(k-1)$-uniform hypergraph $H$ on $n$ vertices, one can count the number of $k$-hypercliques in $H$ in $O(n^{k-\varepsilon_k})$ time. This refutes the hyperclique conjecture of Lincoln, Vassilevska Williams, and Williams (SODA 2018). Our result follows from the uniform construction of a family of arithmetic circuits of size $O(n^{k-\varepsilon_k})$ for the $k$-hyperclique tensor, a natural higher-order generalization of the matrix multiplication tensor. We obtain two corollaries. First, for every $k$, there exists $\varepsilon > 0$ such that Max-$k$SAT can be solved in $2^{(1-\varepsilon)n} \cdot \mathrm{poly}(m,n)$ time. Second, for every $k$, there exists $\varepsilon > 0$ such that arithmetic progressions of length $k$ in subsets of $\{0,1,\ldots,n\}$ can be detected in $n^{2-\varepsilon}$ time. Both corollaries refute other prominent conjectures in the literature.
item.dc:creator: Josh Alman, Baitian Li, Neha Pant, Kevin Pratt, Ryan Williams

item.title: Universal Hardness From Masking Channels
item.description: arXiv:2611.05296v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We prove a broad learning-theoretic generalization of the celebrated hardcore lemma concerning the average-case complexity of computing a Boolean function (Impagliazzo, 1995). Our starting point is the observation that the classic notion of a hardcore measure, which reweights a function's input distribution, is equivalent to an input-dependent masking channel that injects randomness into the function's output distribution until it appears fully pseudorandom. The analogue of density of the measure is the fidelity of the channel. From this viewpoint, we develop a general framework for certifying hardness that allows for non-Boolean functions $f$ and a wide range of notions of hardness besides the classic 0-1 loss, by choosing the right notion of fidelity via convex duality. We show the difficulty of learning $f$ using a class $\mathcal{C}$ to minimize a convex loss is tightly characterized by the maximum fidelity possible for a masking channel, which measures the least amount of noise the channel must add to hide the structure of $f$ and make it $\mathcal{C}$-indistinguishable from random noise. Using our framework, we derive a number of multiclass generalizations of the hardcore lemma, and reveal some unexpected subtleties in going to larger alphabets. We construct a universal masking channel that applies to many natural notions of hardness simultaneously. Such channels are dual to omnipredictors, which optimize multiple losses at once (Gopalan, Kalai, Reingold, Sharan, and Wieder, 2022). We observe a symmetry between masking channels and generalizations of the hardcore lemma using pseudoentropy. We present a tight characterization of pseudoentropy using the MaxEnt algorithm from machine learning. A long line of research has shown that learning and hardness are two sides of the same coin; our framework gives a crisp and general formulation of this principle via convex duality.
item.dc:creator: Parikshit Gopalan, Manoj Prabhakaran, Pranay Tankala

item.title: Quantum Advantage has Few Complexity Implications
item.description: arXiv:2611.05303v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We consider the complexity implications of proofs of quantumness and (quantum verifier) oblivious state preparation. We show that both of these objects can coexist with the easiness of nondeterministic computation. That is, we give evidence that proofs of quantumness can exist when $\mathsf{P} = \mathsf{NP}$ and that (quantum verifier) oblivious state preparation can exist when $\mathsf{BQP} = \mathsf{QCMA}$. In particular, we give a classical oracle relative to which (1) $\mathsf{P}^\mathcal{O} = \mathsf{NP}^\mathcal{O}$ (2) $\mathsf{BQP}^\mathcal{O} = \mathsf{PSPACE}^\mathcal{O}$ (3) Proofs of quantumness exist. In particular, there exists a language in $\mathsf{IP}^\mathcal{O} \subseteq \mathsf{BQP}^\mathcal{O}$ which is hard on average against $\mathsf{P}^\mathcal{O}/poly$. We give a unitary oracle such that (1) $\mathsf{BQP}^\mathcal{O} = \mathsf{QCMA}^\mathcal{O}$ (2) Quantum verifier oblivious state preparation exists. These oracle separations directly imply a number of related consequences. For example, our first result implies that proofs of quantumness cannot be used to construct classical or quantum cryptography with a relativizing proof. Our second result implies that quantum computation/classical communication oblivious transfer cannot be used to construct post-quantum one-way functions with a relativizing proof.
item.dc:creator: Eli Goldin, Alex Lombardi, Tomoyuki Morimae

item.title: Agnostic Learning by Imitating
item.description: arXiv:2611.05346v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Given a class of machine learning models and sample access to a data distribution with binary labels, which computational task is harder: training a discriminative model that distinguishes positive and negative labels as well as the best member of the class, or training a generative model whose outputs are indistinguishable from real data by all members of the class? We prove that these two fundamental tasks in computational learning theory are not just closely related, but actually equivalent to each other in complexity. One direction of this equivalence was previously known. Indeed, the powerful regularity lemma in complexity theory gives an efficient oracle reduction from the indistinguishability task (a.k.a. multiaccuracy) to the distinguishing task (a.k.a. agnostic learning) in the style of boosting algorithms. Our main contribution is an efficient oracle reduction in the other direction. Taking this idea further, we show that a multiaccuracy oracle is a remarkably powerful primitive, achieving not just agnostic learning but also a wide range of seemingly more demanding learning objectives via similarly efficient and direct constructions. Our results crucially use the power of making adaptive queries to the oracle, and stand in stark contrast to prior work, which showed that post-processing a single multiaccurate predictor is insufficient for even weak forms of learning. On a technical level, we draw a connection between our (offline) problem and a version of no-regret learning in the online setting, which allows us to use follow-the-leader type algorithms to modify the label distribution and aggregate the predictions of the multiaccuracy oracle.
item.dc:creator: S\'ilvia Casacuberta, Parikshit Gopalan, Varun Kanade, Omer Reingold, Konstantinos Stavropoulos, Pranay Tankala

item.title: Breaking the quantum barriers for Graph Collision
item.description: arXiv:2611.05356v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In the graph collision problem, the task is to decide whether a known graph on $n$ vertices contains an edge with both endpoints marked, given query access to the input bits specifying the marked vertices. We first refute the conjectured $\Omega(n^{2/3})$ query lower bound with a bounded error quantum algorithm using $\widetilde O(n^{92/139})$ queries. We then refine this approach to obtain a $\widetilde O(n^{11/17})$ query algorithm. We also obtain a $\widetilde O((nq)^{11/17})$ query bound for all (partial) Boolean output functions with positive certificate complexity at most 2 and alphabet size $q$, contrasting a known $\Omega(n^{2/3})$ lower bound for such problems with large alphabet sizes. We complement these algorithms with an $\Omega(\sqrt{n\log n})$ quantum query lower bound for graph collision, exceeding the $O(\sqrt n)$ certificate complexity barrier for the positive adversary method.
item.dc:creator: Arjan Cornelissen, Amin Shiraz Gilani, Shiva Kintali, Fran\c{c}ois Le Gall, Subhasree Patro, Xingyu Zhou

item.title: On the average-case complexity landscape for Tensor-Isomorphism-complete problems over finite fields
item.description: arXiv:2604.00591v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In Grochow and Qiao (\emph{SIAM J. Comput.}, 2023), the complexity class Tensor Isomorphism (TI) was introduced and isomorphism problems for groups, algebras, and polynomials were shown to be TI-complete. In this paper, we study average-case algorithms for several TI-complete problems over finite fields, including algebra isomorphism, matrix code conjugacy, and $4$-tensor isomorphism. Our main results reveal a rich landscape of average-case complexities of Tensor Isomorphism problems, despite their equivalence in the worst-case setting. Over the finite field of order $q$, we devise (1) average-case \emph{polynomial-time} algorithms for algebra isomorphism and matrix code conjugacy that succeed for $1/\Theta(q)$ fraction of inputs; (2) an average-case \emph{polynomial-time} algorithm for the $4$-tensor isomorphism that succeeds for $1/q^{\Theta(1)}$ fraction of inputs; and (3) an average-case \emph{polynomial-time} algorithm for the orthogonal $3$-tensor isomorphism that succeed for $1-1/\poly(n)$ fraction of $n\times n\times n$ tensors. Our main technical contribution is to introduce the spectral properties of random matrices into algorithms for TI-complete problems. This leads to not only new algorithms but also new questions in random matrix theory over finite fields. To settle these questions, we need to extend both the generating function approach as in Neumann and Praeger (\emph{J. London Math. Soc.}, 1998) and the character sum method of Gorodetsky and Rodgers (\emph{Trans. Amer. Math. Soc.}, 2021).
item.dc:creator: Tiange Li, Yinan Li, Youming Qiao, Dacheng Tao, Yingjie Wang

item.title: Constant-factor approximation of MinCostCSP with a conservative majority polymorphism
item.description: arXiv:2607.10667v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: For a relational structure A, the Minimum Cost Constraint Satisfaction Problem is the following problem denoted by MinCostCSP(A): Given an instance of CSP(A) with rational costs on variable-value pairs, find a solution to the instance minimizing the sum of the chosen costs. For the exact minimization, a classification of MinCostCSP(A) in terms of A was established by Takhanov [STACS'10]. We focus on constant-factor approximations of MinCostCSP(A). DeHaan, Huang, and Lee recently showed that if A fails to admit a conservative near-unanimity polymorphism then MinCostCSP(A) is not constant-factor approximable [APPROX'25]. We provide a significant step towards a full classification, by proving a dichotomy for structures A admitting a conservative majority (also known as 3-near-unanimity) polymorphism. Our dichotomy criterion is not in terms of an algebraic condition on A but we show that this is unavoidable. We include a simple argument proving that no such condition exists.
item.dc:creator: Marcin Kozik, Stanislav \v{Z}ivn\'y

item.title: Rigorous Low-Degree Implications for Planted Subgraph Detection: Noise and Treewidth
item.description: arXiv:2608.06279v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The low-degree method predicts computational thresholds by asking whether low-degree polynomials can distinguish a planted distribution from a null one. Recent counterexamples by Buhai, Hsieh, Jain, and Kothari (FOCS 2025) and Mao (2026) show that low-degree indistinguishability does not, in general, rule out efficient algorithms, even on noisy inputs. Hsieh, Kane, Kothari, Li, Mohanty, and Tiegel (STOC 2026) asked what it does imply, and showed that for permutation-invariant distributions on $\{0,1\}^n$, low-degree indistinguishability from the uniform distribution implies statistical indistinguishability after noise. In this work, we study the same question for planted subgraphs in sparse random graphs. Let $Q_n=G(n,c/n)$, and let $P_n$ be obtained by planting a uniformly random copy of a deterministic graph $\Gamma_n$ into an independent sample from $Q_n$. In the supercritical regime $c>1$, we show that if $P_n$ is degree-$D_n$ indistinguishable from $Q_n$ and the treewidth of $\Gamma_n$ is $o(D_n/\log n)$, then a noisy version of $P_n$ is asymptotically indistinguishable from $Q_n$. In the critical and subcritical regimes $0<c\le 1$, we obtain the same conclusion without any treewidth assumption, provided $D_n=\omega(\log n)$. Our proof has two main ingredients. First, we identify the subgraph-count and automorphism factors in the Fourier expansion with counts of isomorphism triples. Second, we cut a tree decomposition of $\Gamma_n$ into subtrees, which splits each large Fourier support into low-degree pieces that meet at only a few interface vertices, and we use noise to absorb the cost of reassembling them. At and below criticality, we use the low-degree assumption to rule out short cycles and noise to destroy the remaining long ones.
item.dc:creator: Xuan Chen, Shuangping Li

item.title: Pseudorandom Functions in $\mathsf{NC}^1$ from LWE/LPN/CDH (Or: How to Build Low-Depth PRFs, Generically)
item.dc:creator: Youlong Ding, Aayush Jain, Ilan Komargodski

item.title: Random Garbage Creates Exponential Quantum Query Separations
item.description: arXiv:2609.03628v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We prove an exponential separation between standard (XOR) quantum queries and forward-erasing queries for a Boolean property of injective functions, answering a question of Aaronson~\cite{Aaronson2021Open}. We also obtain an exponential separation for a Boolean promise problem on permutations, where forward in-place queries are unitary but inverse queries are not supplied. Our construction follows Aaronson's suggestion of appending fixed random garbage to a Simon function. Let $X=\{0,1\}^n$ and $N=2^n$. We use the injection $f_{h,r}(x)=(h(x),x,r_x)$, where $h:X\to X$ is promised to be either a permutation or a Simon function, and $r:X\to X$ is an arbitrary tag table that is reused on every query. The resulting problem is solvable with at most $n+2$ standard queries, but requires $\Theta(\sqrt N)$ forward-erasing queries, matching classical collision sampling. Embedding these instances into permutations, with the copy of $x$ replaced by a single bit that keeps the embedding injective, gives a promise problem on permutations of $L=4N^2$ elements that requires $O(\log L)$ standard queries versus $\Theta(L^{1/4})$ forward in-place queries. The lower bounds use the recording method. We replace each query by a nearby contraction that records cells of a purified tag table. After $T$ queries, tracing out the purified tag table yields a sum of positive-semidefinite contributions, each depending on $h$ at no more than $T$ addresses. A query-by-query hybrid bounds the trace-norm difference between the actual and auxiliary final operators by $O(T/\sqrt N)$. Random permutations and random Simon functions have the same restriction distribution on such a set unless it contains a hidden Simon pair, an event of probability $O(T^2/N)$. Consequently, the actual final states in the two cases remain close unless $T=\Omega(\sqrt N)$, giving the required lower bounds.
item.dc:creator: Khaled Elbassioni, Rishikesh Gajjala, Saurabh Ray

item.title: Max Independent Set Remains NP-hard when Excluding a Planar Induced Minor (and More)
item.description: arXiv:2609.11285v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We show that Max Independent Set (MIS) remains NP-hard in graphs excluding the $5 \times 5$ grid as an induced minor. This negatively answers a question of Dallard--Milani\v{c}--\v{S}torgel that has attracted sustained attention, and refutes a conjecture by Gartland and Lokshtanov. Unless $N$-variable 3-SAT can be solved in time $2^{\mathcal O(N^{1-\varepsilon})}$ for some $\varepsilon > 0$, MIS requires $2^{\Omega(n^{1/2-o(1)})}$ time on $n$-vertex graphs in this class. This complements a $2^{\widetilde{O}(n^{2/3})}$-time algorithm on any $H$-induced-minor-free class by Korhonen and Lokshtanov. Exploiting a connection between low twin-width or reduced parameters on one hand and planar-induced-minor-freeness on the other, we further show that 3-Coloring, Feedback Vertex Set and Dominating Set are NP-complete on weakly sparse graphs of reduced component max-leaf (hence twin-width) at most 3, even when a witnessing contraction sequence is given. Classes of bounded reduced component max-leaf (by any constant) and of twin-width at most 3 are known to exclude a fixed planar graph as an induced minor. The 3-Coloring and Feedback Vertex Set results refute more cases of the Gartland--Lokshtanov conjecture, even when the inputs are weakly sparse. The complexity of MIS in weakly sparse graphs excluding a planar induced minor remains open.
item.dc:creator: \'Edouard Bonnet, Yeonsu Chang

item.title: Near-Logarithmic Inapproximability of Parameterized Set Cover
item.description: arXiv:2609.19623v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In the $\gamma$-gap $k$-SetCover problem, we are given a family $\mathcal{S}$ over a universe $U$, and the goal is to distinguish between the case where $\mathcal{S}$ contains $k$ sets covering $U$, and the case where at least $\gamma k$ sets in $\mathcal{S}$ are needed to cover $U$. We show that, for every $k^{\Omega(k^2)}\le\rho\le n^{O(1)}$, it is W[1]-hard to approximate $k$-SetCover within ratio $\Omega\big(\frac{\log\rho}{k^2\log\log\rho}\big)$ on instances with $n$ sets and universe size at most $\rho\log n$. We also show that under the randomized $k$-OV Hypothesis, there is no bounded-error randomized $f(k)n^{o(k)}$-time $o\big(\frac{\log N}{\log\log N}\big)$-approximation algorithm for $k$-SetCover. These results improve on the previous $(\log n)^{1/O(k)}$-inapproximability. For fixed $k$, this matches the polynomial-time $(\ln\rho+O(1))$-approximation up to a $\log\log\rho$ factor. We further establish a connection between small universes and large approximation gaps. We show that for every $1\le\gamma\le\min\big\{\frac{\log u}{\log\log N},\frac{\log u}{k^2\log\log u}\big\}$, exact $k$-SetCover with universe size $u^{\Theta(1/\gamma)}$ is equivalent to $\gamma$-gap $k$-SetCover with universe size $u$ under randomized Turing reductions. This suggests a barrier to proving superconstant-gap W[2]-hardness: such a result would also make exact $k$-SetCover with universe size $n^{o(1)}$ W[2]-hard under randomized FPT Turing reductions. Finally, we analyze the VC dimensions of the set systems produced by our reduction. Write $d$ and $d^*$ for the primal and dual VC dimensions respectively. We show that for $\gamma=o(\frac{\log N}{\log\log N})$, $\gamma$-gap $k$-SetCover is W[1]-hard even when $d=O(k^{2}\gamma\log(k\gamma))$ and $d^*=O(k\gamma)$. The bound for $d^*$ matches the $O(d^*\log k)$-approximation algorithm up to a $k\log k$ factor.
item.dc:creator: Bingkai Lin, Xin Zheng

item.title: FPT iff PTIME for Homomorphism Problems on Sparse-Incidence and Bounded-Independence Patterns
item.description:
arXiv:2609.21840v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We show that fixed-parameter tractability and polynomial-time solvability coincide for homomorphism problems specified by classes of pattern hypergraphs of bounded incidence degeneracy or bounded primal independence number, assuming $FPT 
e W[1]$. In both cases, tractability is characterised by bounded fractional hypertree width. This generalises a result of Grohe [JACM 2007] that established such an FPT-PTIME collapse for bounded-arity structures. We build on the fractional balanced-separator framework and rounding theorem of Korchemna, Lokshtanov, Saurabh, Surianarayanan, and Xue [FOCS 2024] to prove near-linear bounds on fractional hypertree width ($fhw$) in terms of adaptive width ($adw$). Namely, for every hypergraph $H$ $$fhw(H)=O(\mu(H) adw(H)\log adw(H)), \quad fhw(H)=O(\log \alpha(H) adw(H)\log adw(H))$$ where $\mu(H)$ is the degeneracy of the incidence graph of $H$ and $\alpha(H)$ the independence number of the primal graph of $H$. As a consequence, we obtain a corresponding FPT-PTIME collapse for exact homomorphism decision and counting on every class in which either incidence degeneracy or independence number is bounded. This includes a number of natural classes such as pattern hypergraphs of bounded degree. Additionally, we observe that for every r.e. class of pattern hypergraphs, fixed-parameter tractability of the parameterised homomorphism problem implies quasipolynomial-time solvability of the corresponding unparameterised problem, assuming $FPT 
e W[1]$. Our results rely on the characterisation of fixed-parameter tractable decision of homomorphism problems in terms of submodular width of Marx [JACM 2013], conditional on ETH. In light of the very recent potential refutation of the ETH, we show that the characterisation of Marx holds also under the assumption that $FPT 
e W[1]$.
item.dc:creator: Matthias Lanzinger

item.title: An exponential lower bound for the bit pigeonhole principle in resolution over parities
item.description: arXiv:2609.23015v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Resolution over parities, $\mathrm{Res}(\oplus)$, is the characteristic-two version of resolution over linear equations: clauses are disjunctions of affine equations over $\mathbb F_2$. Superpolynomial size lower bounds were previously known only for restricted refutations: tree-like, regular, or of bounded depth. We prove that every DAG-like $\mathrm{Res} (\oplus)$ refutation of the bit pigeonhole principle with $n+1$ pigeons and $n=2^\ell$ holes has more than $\exp(n/(32768\ell^2))=2^{\Omega(n/\log^2 n)}$ clauses, for every $\ell\ge32$, with no restriction on regularity or depth. The proof translates an arbitrary refutation with $S$ clauses into a polynomial calculus refutation of degree $O(\log n)$ over $O(S+n^2)$ groups of extension variables in the style of Buss, Impagliazzo, Krajicek, Pudlak, Razborov, and Sgall. One substitution then removes all extension variables at once and leaves a nonzero low-degree polynomial derived from the pigeonhole axioms alone at degree at most $n/2$; a degree lower bound in the style of Razborov, proved through the homology of chessboard complexes, shows that no such derivation exists. The argument also yields a general sufficient condition for $\mathrm{Res}(\oplus)$ size lower bounds. The main theorem, this condition, and all their dependencies are formalized in Lean 4, and every statement links to its formal proof. The proof was developed with substantial AI assistance within an open research framework described in the final section.
item.dc:creator: Kamil Braun

item.title: A Fixed-Parameter Algorithm for 4-Block Integer Programming
item.description: arXiv:2609.23711v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We give a fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) algorithm with running time $f(k,\bar\Delta)\cdot {|I|}^{O(1)}$ for integer linear programs with 4-block structure, parameterized by the maximum block dimension $k$ and the largest absolute entry $\bar\Delta$ in the local-column blocks. This result resolves a long-standing open question in parameterized complexity, and answers a conjecture by Eisenbrand and Rothvoss (2026) in the positive. This result has several implications for other block-structured integer programming models, including mixed fracture number and special cases of 4-block programs with large entries outside of the diagonal. Important tools for this algorithm are structural properties of generalized $n$-fold integer programs shown by Ligthart~(2026) and an algorithm by Veselov, Gribanov, Zolotykh and Chirkov~(2020) for optimizing discrete convic functions. Independently and shortly after the first version of our paper appeared, Kouteck\'y, Lassota, and Ligthart (2026) obtained an FPT algorithm for 4-block integer programming.
item.dc:creator: Klaus Jansen, Felix Ohnesorge, Corinna Wambsganz

item.title: 4-Block Integer Programming is in FPT
item.description: arXiv:2609.26746v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Integer programming is a fundamental and important NP-hard problem. This motivated extensive efforts in studying several tractable subclasses. One of the most important, unresolved complexity questions is the parameterized complexity of 4-block IPs, a natural class characterized by having a diagonal matrix with small blocks after deleting few rows and columns. Over the years, significant progress has been made in improving algorithms for 4-block IPs, but the question whether such IPs can be solved in FPT time, parameterized by the block dimensions and largest matrix coefficient, has remained open. This question is repeatedly highlighted, most recently by Kouteck\'y [IPEC 2025] and by Eisenbrand and Rothvoss [SODA 2026]. We resolve this question in the positive by providing an FPT time algorithm. Our algorithm can optimize non-linear, separable convex objective functions, and can be extended to broader classes of constraint matrices (such as tree-fold or multi-stage) and allows appending few ``global'' columns to it, and it allows coefficients unbounded by the parameters in those columns. It is known that tractability cannot be extended further in any of those directions. The key structural property that we establish is that a function $f\colon\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb R$ that is integer midpoint convex, i.e., $f(x)\le\tfrac12f(x-p)+\tfrac12f(x+p)$ for all $x,p\in\mathbb Z^n$, can be extended to a convex function on the set $2d\mathbb Z^n\cap L$ if $L$ is a linear subspace of dimension $d$. This closes the gap in a recent work by Ligthart [arXiv 2606.30330, 2026], which allows us to extend the previous algorithm that solves 4-block integer programs with a single global variable to incorporate any parameterized number of global variables. As an example, we apply our algorithm to solve an open problem posed by Boehmer and Koana [ACM Trans. Algorithms, 2024] in Max-Min Fair Matching.
item.dc:creator: Martin Kouteck\'y, Alexandra Lassota, Koen Ligthart

item.title: Pfaffian Recognition is in $\mathsf{coRP}$
item.description: arXiv:2610.29817v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: An orientation of a graph is called Pfaffian if all perfect matchings occur with the same sign in its Pfaffian expansion. A graph is Pfaffian if it admits such an orientation. Given a Pfaffian orientation, the number of perfect matchings can be computed in polynomial time. In 1963, Kasteleyn showed that every planar graph is Pfaffian. In 1989, Vazirani and Yannakakis showed that deciding whether a graph is Pfaffian is polynomial time equivalent to testing whether a given orientation is Pfaffian. For bipartite graphs, polynomial time recognition algorithms were obtained by Robertson, Seymour, and Thomas in 1999, and independently by McCuaig in 2004. Whether a deterministic polynomial time algorithm exists for general graphs remains open. In this paper, we first construct a polynomial that is identically zero if and only if a given orientation is Pfaffian, and show that this polynomial can be evaluated in polynomial time. Combined with the reduction of Vazirani and Yannakakis, this gives a randomized polynomial time algorithm for deciding whether a general graph is Pfaffian, placing the problem in $\mathsf{coRP}$. We also prove that an orientation of a matching covered graph is non-Pfaffian if and only if reversing the edges of some cut makes it strongly connected. Although deciding whether such a cut exists is NP-complete for general digraphs, our characterization yields a randomized polynomial time algorithm for matching covered graphs and deterministic polynomial time algorithms for bipartite and planar matching covered graphs.
item.dc:creator: Priyanshu Pant, Ranveer Singh

item.title: Asymptotic Rank of Weighted Graph Tensors via Completely Positive Covers
item.description: arXiv:2610.34273v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We give a conic upper bound on the asymptotic rank of every weighted graph tensor over every field. If $W$ is the logarithmic edge-weight matrix of its dimension matrix $Q$, then $$ \operatorname{MaxCut}(W)\le\log_2\operatorname{\widetilde R}_{\mathbb F}(\operatorname{WT}(Q))\le U_{\operatorname{CP}}^{\Delta}(W). $$ Here $U_{\operatorname{CP}}^{\Delta}(W)$ maximizes $\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}W_{i,j}P_{i,j}$ over nonnegative symmetric zero-diagonal matrices $P$ such that $J-2P$ is copositive and $P_{i,j}\le P_{i,k}+P_{k,j}$ for all distinct vertices. The matrix $J$ is all-one, and copositivity means nonnegativity of the quadratic form on nonnegative vectors. Our starting point extends OpenAI's polynomial multiplication method and its subsequent arbitrary-field developments from three tensor legs to arbitrary order. We prove $$ \left\lfloor\frac{n^2}{4}\right\rfloor\le\log_2\operatorname{\widetilde R}_{\mathbb F}(\operatorname{GT}_2(K_n))\le\frac{n^2}{4}. $$ The edge exponent is at most $n/(2(n-1))$ and tends to the optimal value $1/2$, improving the previous Coppersmith--Winograd bounds and answering Question 1.3.1 of Christandl, Vrana, and Zuiddam. The bounds coincide for every even $n$. For every odd $m\ge3$, the theorem gives $\log_2\widetilde R_{\mathbb F}(\operatorname{GT}_2(C_m))\le m-1+1/(m+1)$, improving the previous cycle bound with a gap of only $1/(m+1)$ above the maximum cut. On weighted triangles, the program recovers the rectangular matrix multiplication curve of Uzna\'nski and Amanov, van den Berg, and Zuiddam. The CP and semidefinite programs, with or without path constraints, all have value $9/4$ on the unweighted triangle, giving this upper bound a natural conic interpretation. Further applications give explicit bounds for complete multipartite graphs, split graphs, and wheels, including new cases of maximum-cut equality.
item.dc:creator: Huanyi Zhou

item.title: How Hard Is It to Compute Cover Time?
item.description: arXiv:2610.38998v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: It is $\#\mathrm{P}$-hard. Even for connected simple undirected unweighted graphs, deciding whether an expected random-walk cover time is at most a given rational threshold is $\#\mathrm{P}$-hard under polynomial-time Turing reductions, both from a specified starting vertex and when maximized over starting vertices. Hardness holds even for graphs of diameter two with a universal vertex, which we call the "hub". Deleting the hub leaves a planar bipartite graph, and every non-hub vertex has degree at most five. A shared construction encodes an Euler-tour count in rare covering walks. For specified starts, a number of fractional bits linear in the queried graph's vertex count suffices to recover the Euler-tour count. For the maximum-start problem, a fixed cube attachment makes the maximizing starts known, and one finite-difference calculation on expected cover times recovers the count. For general graphs, both comparison problems can be solved in polynomial time with access to an $\mathrm{NP}^{\mathrm{PP}}$ oracle.

item.title: Quantifier Elimination Meets Treewidth
item.description: arXiv:2601.00312v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In this paper, we address the complexity barrier inherent in Fourier-Motzkin elimination (FME) and cylindrical algebraic decomposition (CAD) when eliminating a block of (existential) quantifiers. To mitigate this, we propose exploiting structural sparsity in the variable dependency graph of quantified formulas. Utilizing tools from parameterized algorithms, we investigate the role of treewidth, a parameter that measures the graph's tree-likeness, in the process of quantifier elimination. A novel dynamic programming framework, structured over a tree decomposition of the dependency graph, is developed for applying FME and CAD, and is also extensible to general quantifier elimination procedures. Crucially, we prove that when the treewidth is a constant, the framework achieves a significant exponential complexity improvement for both FME and CAD, reducing the worst-case complexity bound from doubly exponential to single exponential. Preliminary experiments on sparse linear real arithmetic (LRA) and nonlinear real arithmetic (NRA) benchmarks confirm that our algorithm outperforms the existing popular heuristic-based approaches on instances exhibiting low treewidth.
item.dc:creator: Hao Wu, Jiyu Zhu, Amir Kafshdar Goharshady, Jie An, Bican Xia, Naijun Zhan

item.title: Statistical and Computational Limits for Cumulant Tensor Inference: A Regime in Which Efficient Detection Is Harder Than Efficient Estimation
item.description: arXiv:2603.26029v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study estimation and detection of high-order cumulant tensors from $n$ i.i.d. observations of a $p$-dimensional random vector, with performance measured in the tensor spectral norm. Under sub-Gaussianity, we show that the minimax rate for estimating the order-$d$ cumulant tensor is $\sqrt{p/n}\wedge 1$. In contrast to covariance estimation, the natural plug-in estimator obtained by replacing population moments in the moment--cumulant formula with sample moments, which we call the sample cumulant tensor, is generally not rate-optimal for $d\ge 3$, and we construct an estimator that attains the minimax rate. On the computational side, we study testing whether the $d$-th order cumulant tensor vanishes after whitening. We provide evidence, under a model-specific low-degree conjecture, that detection is computationally hard when $n\ll p^{d/2}$. At the same time, we identify a regime in which an efficiently computable estimator achieves error smaller than the separation at which polynomial-time tests can reliably distinguish the null from the alternative under the same conjecture. This reveals an unusual reverse detection--estimation gap: computationally efficient detection can be harder than computationally efficient estimation. The underlying reason is that the relevant loss, tensor spectral norm, is itself NP-hard to compute, creating a new form of computational--statistical gap.
item.dc:creator: Runshi Tang, Yuefeng Han, Anru R. Zhang

item.title: How Does Machine Learning Manage Complexity?
item.description: arXiv:2604.07233v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We provide a computational complexity lens to understand the power of machine learning models, particularly their ability to model complex systems. Machine learning models are often trained on data drawn from sampleable or more complex distributions, a far wider range of distributions than just computable ones. By focusing on computable distributions, machine learning models can better manage complexity via probability. We abstract away from specific learning mechanisms, modeling machine learning as producing P/poly-computable distributions with polynomially-bounded max-entropy. We illustrate how learning computable distributions models complexity by showing that if a machine learning model produces a distribution $\mu$ that models the distribution generated by a cryptographic pseudorandom generator at least as well as the uniform distribution does, then $\mu$ must be close to uniform. We view training as compression that removes the randomness from the data, keeping only its structure, and inference as adding randomness back to generate new outputs. A computationally bounded model cannot distinguish pseudorandomness from true randomness, so training removes both, treating anything it cannot efficiently predict as noise. The same holds at inference, where the randomness added back can be, and in practice is, pseudorandom. In the appendix, we make the connection to compression precise and, using a characterization of pseudoentropy by Vadhan and Zheng, show that the best loss achievable by an efficient model is the next-bit pseudoentropy of the data.
item.dc:creator: Lance Fortnow

item.title: A Near-Linear Element-Kernel for \(d\)-Hitting Set
item.description: arXiv:2609.06512v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In \(d\)-Hitting Set, the input consists of a finite universe \(U\), a family \(\mathcal S\) of subsets of \(U\) with size at most \(d\), and an integer \(k\). The task is to decide whether at most \(k\) elements of \(U\) can intersect every set in \(\mathcal S\). Previously known kernels contain \(O(k^{d-1})\) elements and \(O(k^d)\) sets. Whether the number of elements can be reduced to \(O(k^{d-1-\varepsilon})\) for some constant \(\varepsilon>0\) is a longstanding open problem in kernelization. In this paper, we answer this question affirmatively by giving a near-linear randomized element-kernel and a subquadratic deterministic element-kernel through a re-encoding of the instance. For every fixed \(d\geq3\), we give a one-sided randomized kernel with \(O_d(k\log^3k)\) elements and a deterministic kernel with \(O_d(k^{7/4}\log^{3/2}k)\) elements. Our kernels may still contain \(k^{O(d)}\) sets and the parameter \(k\) may grow polynomially.

item.title: Word Length and Diameter in Permutation Groups
item.description: arXiv:2609.26307v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In the binary diameter problem, the input consists of explicitly given permutations generating a finite group $G$ and a binary-encoded number $k$, and the question is whether every element of $G$ is a product of at most $k$ of the given generators. In the binary length problem, the input additionally contains a permutation $g \in G$, and the question is whether $g$ is such a product. We show that the binary diameter problem is PSPACE-complete, thereby confirming a conjecture of Lohrey and Rosowski (2023). Moreover, we show that PSPACE-hardness already holds for solvable groups of derived length at most 3, whereas the problem is $\Pi_2^{\mathrm{P}}$-complete for 2-step nilpotent groups. For the binary length problem, we establish a sharp complexity threshold: the problem is NP-complete for 2-step nilpotent groups, which extends a result of Lohrey and Rosowski for abelian groups, and PSPACE-complete for groups that are simultaneously 3-step nilpotent and metabelian, which strengthens the main result of Jerrum (1985). Finally, we show that the unary diameter problem, where $k$ is encoded in unary, is $\Pi_2^{\mathrm{P}}$-complete for generating sets of the full symmetric group, confirming another conjecture of Lohrey and Rosowski.

item.title: Exponential quantum space advantage in random data streams
item.description: arXiv:2610.03645v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We show two unconditional quantum space advantages in the random-order streaming model. First, we show the Yamakawa-Zhandry Code Intersection problem admits exponential quantum advantage in the streaming model when its inputs are streamed in random order. This means quantum computers exhibit exponential space advantage even when simply receiving $(x,f(x))$ pairs for a uniformly random function $f$ in a uniformly random order. Notably, our classical space lower bound does not follow from a communication lower bound. Instead, we utilize density-restoring partitions from communication complexity directly with potential-function analysis in the style used to prove memory-sample tradeoffs for learning. The resulting argument is distinct from both lines of work. Second, we use our framework to show quantum space advantage for the Optimal Polynomial Intersection (OPI) problem in certain regimes via a streaming version of the Decoded Quantum Interferometry algorithm. In particular, we show that for degree $d$ and $n$ evaluation points, attaining $1/2 + \Omega(\sqrt{d/n})$ fraction of satisfied OPI constraints via streaming requires $\Omega(n)$ classical bits of memory but only $O(d\log n)$ qubits. This yields provable quantum advantage in a "low-rate" regime when the number of evaluation points is much larger than the degree, with a space advantage that can be as large as exponential in certain parameter settings.
item.dc:creator: Adam Bouland, Matthew Ding, Siddhartha Jain

item.title: An FPRAS for Counting Common Bases of Two Matroids
item.description: arXiv:2610.06724v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We design the first fully polynomial-time randomized approximation scheme ($\mathsf{FPRAS}$) for approximately counting and uniformly sampling common bases of two matroids given by their independence oracles. Moreover, our algorithms generalize far beyond this to Hadamard products of two probability measures on the Boolean cube satisfying a simple nonnegative curvature condition. These algorithmic primitives have myriad applications in statistical physics, polyhedral combinatorics, the theory of quantum many-body systems, and beyond. The central difficulty is that the hard constraints imposed by the two input matroids (or the two input measures, more generally) obstruct traditional approaches based on local Markov chains. Relaxing these constraints can restore rapid mixing, but configurations that satisfy the original hard constraints may become exponentially rare if this is done na\"ively. Our main contribution is a novel approach for approximate counting that marries Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) with convex programming to overcome these obstacles: - We relax the intersection by imposing an overlap penalty on the product measure formed by the two input measures. We prove, via an integrated Bochner-type method, that this "soft intersection" satisfies a Poincar\'e Inequality uniformly over all external fields. - We use samples from the relaxed distribution to solve a dual maximum entropy convex program inspired by the Gurvits capacity. This program reweights the soft intersection measure using external fields to boost the aggregate probability of configurations satisfying the hard intersection constraint, without changing their relative weights. We bound the success probability directly using the uniform Poincar\'e Inequality and smallness of the gradient norm. item.title: Nearly optimal Personalized PageRank computation
item.description: arXiv:2610.06959v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the fundamental problem of computing Personalized PageRank (PPR) on an undirected and unweighted graph $G$. We focus on the $\eps$-error guarantee introduced by Andersen, Chung, and Lang [ACL; FOCS 2006 $\&$ Internet Math 2007]. Their classic local push method computes an approximate PPR vector satisfying the ACL $\eps$-error guarantee in $O((\alpha\eps)^{-1})$ time, where $\alpha$ is the teleportation parameter. This problem has a lower bound $\Omega(\eps^{-1})$. Working with idealized SDDM solves, we eliminate the dependence on $\alpha$ and present an algorithm that achieves the same error guarantee in $O(\eps^{-1-o(1)})$ time. Consequently, we obtain a nearly optimal algorithm for PPR computation under the ACL error guarantee, and a nearly linear algorithm for local graph clustering with complexity independent of $\phi$.

item.title: Unconditional Boolean Dynamic Lower Bounds from Disjointness
item.description: arXiv:2610.10904v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We prove an unconditional $\Omega((\log n/\log\log n)^2)$ lower bound on the maximum of the worst-case update time and expected query time for the insert-only version of Patrascu's multiphase Disjointness problem [STOC 2010]. The bound holds in the zero-error cell-probe model with logarithmic word size. Patrascu's reductions transfer it to directed reachability under edge insertions, already on directed acyclic graphs of depth $2$. This improves the $\widetilde{\Omega}(\log^{3/2} n)$ bound of Larsen and Yu [SICOMP 2025] to the quadratic-logarithmic scale previously attained for dynamic range counting and multiphase Inner Product. The bound also transfers to a broad collection of dynamic graph, algebraic, geometric, and string problems. We also obtain a separation between amortized and worst-case time for streaming regular-expression membership. For a simple family of expressions of maximum length $M$ over a polynomial-size alphabet, a deterministic algorithm uses $O(1)$ amortized time per symbol on every input stream, whereas every zero-error cell-probe algorithm with word size $w=\Theta(\log M)$ requires $\Omega((\log M/\log\log M)^2)$ time on some symbol. The proof adapts Ko's 2.5-round multiphase communication framework [FOCS 2026] from Inner Product to Disjointness. Our main technical observation is that the protocol's verification step allows a one-sided corruption bound to replace the discrepancy property used for Inner Product.
